Lessons.Title: Two-way Tables
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: construct and interpret two-way tables for two categorical variables, calculate missing marginal counts and explain what a selected cell means. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U03:L01, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/3/1/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0); publisher Addressing HSS-ID.B.5. The source uses preference data and a partner information-gap activity, not numerical measurements alone.

Original hypothetical survey: two fictional groups A and B each contain 20 responses about Sports versus Arts as preferred club. Group A: 12 Sports,8 Arts; Group B: 9 Sports,11 Arts. Column totals Sports21, Arts19; grand total40. The table has two categorical variables (group and club), with numerical frequencies counting responses.

Student task: reconstruct a partially hidden table by asking a partner which row and column totals are known, calculate missing cells, interpret counts in words, and justify how totals expose a miscopied entry. Do not claim responses came from actual classmates. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correctly structured and labelled table, accurate internal/marginal/grand totals, clear interpretation and reasoned information-gap questions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Categorical variable
KeyConcepts.Definition: A characteristic whose values are group labels rather than measured amounts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Treat labels separately from count frequencies.
KeyConcepts.Example: Group A/B and Sports/Arts are two categorical variables.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two-way count
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each interior cell counts observations in the intersection of a row and column.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A person appears once under each categorical variable.

KeyConcepts.Title: Marginal total
KeyConcepts.Definition: Row/column totals are sums of their interior cells.
KeyConcepts.Rule: All row and column grand totals must match.

WorkedExamples.Title: Calculate row and column totals
WorkedExamples.Question: Complete A=(12 Sports,8 Arts), B=(9 Sports,11 Arts).
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a cell without denominators
WorkedExamples.Question: What does the entry 9 mean?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: Locate row B and column Sports.
Read nine counted responses at this intersection.
The variable describes preference, not nine sports events.
Do not infer anything about other survey populations.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Nine hypothetical Group B respondents preferred Sports.
WorkedExamples.Check: Cell cannot imply actual group member identities.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a missing count
WorkedExamples.Question: If A totals20 and A Sports12, find A Arts.
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the first-party data, compute with the correct denominator, and interpret with sample limitations.
Steps: Use the A row count equation 12+x=20.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both row and column totals agree.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding row totals and column totals to get the grand total
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose one direction of marginal totals.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating group names as numerical measurements
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Categories are labels even when counts are numbers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify response types separately from their frequencies.

SummaryPoints: Two-way tables organize two categorical variables simultaneously.
Every observation contributes to one row-column intersection.
Row totals and column totals reconcile to the same grand total.
Teacher scores questions and interpretation; no class survey data are fabricated.
